assumptions: The initial service can be structured as security-evidence preparation without advising on, arranging, or selling insurance unless performed through a licensed partner.
Target Polish broker questionnaires materially overlap the control categories shown in the cited current international application materials.
Clients can grant access to the necessary technical evidence and consent to a secure handoff to their chosen licensed broker.
Remediation requiring privileged system access is performed by qualified MSP or security partners rather than silently included in verification.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Written regulatory-boundary advice; acceptance criteria and pilot commitments from at least three licensed Polish brokers; ten paid SME sprints; measured completion time, expert-review cost, remediation conversion, gross margin, and annual-refresh intent; plus before-and-after submission, turnaround, quotation, or coverage outcomes.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Cyber-insurance applications require operational evidence about controls such as MFA, patching, backups, training, incidents, and encryption, while many SMEs lack internal security staff. Converting that pre-underwriting burden into a fixed-scope verified evidence pack is a clear workflow product, although insurer acceptance and quote impact in Poland are not yet demonstrated.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: A first application, renewal, rejected submission, customer contract, or lender condition creates a deadline and an identifiable cost of incomplete evidence. The cited forms validate work to be done but not Polish SME willingness to pay 2,500-7,500 PLN or that a readiness sprint changes coverage, premium, or placement speed.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: A prepaid fixed-price sprint has low capital needs, clear scope, and the potential for software-assisted gross margin; an annual refresh adds repeat revenue without carrying insurance risk. Reviewer labor, remediation coordination, acquisition share, professional liability, support, and refresh conversion remain unmeasured, and legally permissible channel compensation is unresolved.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish SMEs without internal security teams form a plausible broad market, and rejected or deadline-bound applicants offer a focused trigger. The candidate does not quantify insured or seeking-to-insure SMEs, broker submission fallout, vertical differences, control maturity, or a first broker and customer segment with sufficient volume.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: A reusable, broker-accepted evidence artifact could be more objective and bounded than open-ended security consulting. MSPs already administer the relevant systems, brokers can provide questionnaires, security consultants can verify controls, and any of them can internalize a standardized checklist unless acceptance or workflow integration creates a stronger position.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: The service can extend from first-time applications to renewals, control refreshes, remediation routing, customer-contract evidence, lender requirements, and multiple broker channels. Expansion toward broader managed security would increase labor and competition, while insurer-specific forms can fragment rather than compound the product.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Permissioned mappings from evidence gaps to remediation time and quote outcomes could improve triage and become valuable if brokers supply outcome feedback. No right to that outcome data or privileged broker workflow is secured, the distribution agreement would be nonexclusive, and checklists plus evidence collection are readily reproducible.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Data-science and finance skills fit questionnaire normalization, evidence scoring, and outcome analysis, and the model can begin with public forms and low capital. The founder has no demonstrated security credentials, Polish broker appointment, SME pipeline, insurer acceptance, or proprietary underwriting data.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Current underwriting workflows ask detailed questions about security controls, making evidence preparation a live rather than speculative task, and recurring cyber incidents reinforce attention to insurability. The cited requirements are international and do not establish identical Polish underwriting practice or a durable rise in local paid demand.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Brokers, MSPs, accountants, and lenders can all encounter the customer at a credible purchase trigger, and a white-label fixed-scope sprint is channel-friendly. None of those channels is contracted, brokers retain the insurance relationship, referral compensation may be regulated, and MSPs may prefer to deliver the work themselves.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A ten-client, standardized readiness pilot with remediation referred out is operationally feasible within the stated time and capital. Sensitive evidence creates security and liability exposure, verification can be mistaken for a guarantee, technical review quality matters, and the boundary between readiness support and regulated insurance distribution requires explicit legal design.

highest_value_structural_change: Make the product a formally accepted white-label intake protocol for one licensed Polish broker and one MSP channel, with contracted minimum referral volume and permission to learn from de-identified submission and quote outcomes while keeping insurance advice and placement with the broker.
main_structural_strength: The offer attaches a finite, auditable service to a deadline-driven underwriting event and can create a reusable evidence asset instead of delivering undifferentiated cyber consulting.
primary_score_limiter: There is no proof that licensed Polish brokers will accept the third-party pack, that it improves quotation outcomes, or that SMEs will pay enough to support secure expert verification and channel acquisition.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: The cited underwriting materials are international rather than evidence of Polish acceptance criteria, and the MSP already controlling an SME's systems may be able to assemble the same evidence more cheaply while retaining the customer relationship.
